clinicalPearls: C. perfringens myonecrosis (gas gangrene) is one of the most fulminant gram-positive bacterial infections of humans; it is a true emergency requiring immediate surgical debridement and is invariably fatal if untreated (p.1241).

Traumatic gas gangrene presents with sudden onset of excruciating pain at the affected site and rapid development of a foul-smelling wound with thin serosanguineous discharge and gas bubbles; brawny edema and induration give way to cutaneous blisters with bluish to maroon-colored fluid (p.1241).

The patient's pain and toxic appearance are characteristically out of proportion to physical findings; the patient may be febrile, apathetic, tachycardic, tachypneic, and may express a feeling of impending doom (p.1218, cross-ref Chap.159).

The margin between healthy and necrotic tissue often advances several inches per hour despite appropriate antibiotic therapy; radical amputation remains the single best life-saving intervention (p.1241).
Incubation period for traumatic gas gangrene can be as short as 6 h and is usually <4 days (p.1241).

Spontaneous (nontraumatic) gas gangrene arises by hematogenous seeding of normal muscle, principally with C. septicum (aerotolerant), C. perfringens, and C. novyi, from a gastrointestinal portal of entry (p.1241).
First symptom of spontaneous gas gangrene may be confusion followed by abrupt onset of excruciating pain in the absence of trauma; with fever, these findings should heighten suspicion (p.1242).

Gram staining of drainage or tissue biopsy is usually definitive in traumatic disease, showing large gram-positive (or gram-variable) rods, an ABSENCE of inflammatory cells, and widespread soft tissue necrosis (p.1241).
CT and MRI help determine whether infection is localized or spreading along fascial planes, but must NOT replace surgical exploration, Gram's staining, and histopathologic examination (p.1242).

Emergent thorough surgical debridement with wide resection back to healthy viable muscle and skin is of extreme importance; closure of traumatic wounds or compound fractures should be delayed 5-6 days until sites are certain to be free of infection (p.1242).
harrison.pathophysiology: Development requires an anaerobic environment and wound contamination with clostridial spores or vegetative organisms. Devitalized tissue, foreign bodies, and ischemia lower local oxygen and favor outgrowth. For C. perfringens and C. novyi, trauma must be sufficient to interrupt the blood supply to establish the anaerobic niche; the more aerotolerant C. septicum and C. tertium can seed normal tissue from GI lesions without this. Once established, organisms proliferate and elaborate exotoxins. The major C. perfringens toxins in gas gangrene are alpha toxin (a lethal hemolysin with phospholipase C and sphingomyelinase activity; the major virulence factor) and theta toxin (perfringolysin, a cholesterol-dependent cytolysin). Severe pain, rapid progression, marked tissue destruction, and the characteristic paucity of neutrophils in tissue are largely attributable to alpha-toxin-induced vascular occlusion by heterotypic platelet/neutrophil aggregates (via activation of platelet gpIIb/IIIa). Late cardiovascular collapse reflects theta toxin causing reduced systemic vascular resistance with increased cardiac output ('warm shock') and alpha toxin directly suppressing myocardial contractility, producing profound hypotension (p.1242).
infectionMimics: Necrotizing fasciitis (including type I polymicrobial and C. perfringens necrotizing fasciitis); distinction from clostridial myonecrosis is made by muscle biopsy (p.1218/1241)
Other histotoxic clostridial necrotizing soft tissue infections (C. histolyticum, C. septicum, C. novyi, C. sordellii) (p.1241)
Synergistic necrotizing cellulitis / crepitant (crepitus) cellulitis due to mixed anaerobic and aerobic flora (p.gas-forming soft-tissue infections)
Fournier's gangrene (C. perfringens with mixed aerobic/anaerobic microbes can cause aggressive type I necrotizing fasciitis or Fournier's gangrene) (p.1239)
Clostridial sepsis / bacteremia with myonecrosis (grave prognosis when bacteremia accompanies myonecrosis) (p.1240)
nonInfectiousMimics: Gas tracking/dissecting tissue planes from non-clostridial gas-forming processes; note gas gangrene may develop in the ABSENCE of clostridial infection (other gas-producing organisms) (p.crepitus/gas-forming infections)
additionalInvestigations: Gram stain of a smear of involved tissue (direct examination is of major importance): large gram-positive/gram-variable rods with paucity of leukocytes (p.1242)

Surgical exploration with histopathologic examination (widespread tissue destruction, paucity of leukocytes in infected tissue with accumulation of leukocytes in adjacent vessels, gram-positive rods with or without spores) (p.1242)
Blood cultures (anaerobic) - obtain when spontaneous gas gangrene is suspected, as bacteremia usually precedes cutaneous manifestations by several hours (p.1242)
CT and MRI to define localized vs fascial-plane spread (adjunct only; must not delay surgery) (p.1242)
Needle aspiration or punch biopsy may provide an etiologic diagnosis in at least 20% of cases (p.1242)
In survivors of C. septicum bacteremia/spontaneous gangrene: aggressive diagnostic workup to rule out gastrointestinal pathology (e.g., colonic malignancy) (p.1241)
redFlags: Pain out of proportion to physical findings - excruciating pain at the affected site (p.1241/1218)
Crepitus and gas in the tissues / gas on imaging with rapidly progressive necrosis (p.1241-1242)
Tissue margin advancing several inches per hour despite antibiotics (p.1241)
Systemic toxaemia: shock, hypotension, multiorgan failure, bacteremia, intravascular hemolysis (p.1241-1242)
Foul-smelling serosanguineous wound discharge with bluish/maroon hemorrhagic bullae and brawny induration (p.1241)
Spontaneous excruciating pain with confusion and fever and NO obvious portal of entry - suggests spontaneous gas gangrene (correct diagnosis frequently delayed or missed) (p.1242)
Feeling of impending doom with apathy, tachycardia, tachypnea (p.1218)
harrison.prognosis: Invariably fatal if untreated. When patients become bacteremic the mortality rate exceeds 50%. Spontaneous (nontraumatic) gas gangrene mortality ranges from 67-100% in adults and 59% in children (most childhood deaths within 24 h of onset). Prognosis is more favorable when an extremity is involved (easier debridement) than the trunk or visceral organs. Disease is most likely to progress to shock and death in patients with associated bacteremia and intravascular hemolysis; mortality is highest for patients in shock at diagnosis. Gas gangrene associated with bacteremia represents a later stage with the worst outcomes. Survivors may undergo multiple debridements and face prolonged hospitalization and rehabilitation (p.1242-1243).
pitfalls: Diagnosis depends on clinical signs and symptoms, not solely on bacteriologic findings - 30-80% of open traumatic wounds are contaminated with clostridia and clostridia are isolated equally from suppurative and well-healing wounds (p.1239).
In spontaneous gas gangrene the lack of an obvious portal of entry means the correct diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed (p.1242).
Adjunctive procedures (CT, MRI) or transport to hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) units must NOT delay emergent surgical debridement (p.1243).

The value of HBO remains controversial; HBO inhibits C. perfringens but not the more aerotolerant C. septicum, and blood/macerated muscle inhibit its bactericidal potential in vitro - HBO provides benefit only if surgery and antibiotics precede it (p.1243).
Avoid prolonged tourniquet application and surgical closure of contaminated traumatic wounds; patients with compound fractures are at significant risk if the wound is closed surgically (p.1243).

C. perfringens remains largely penicillin-susceptible but clindamycin resistance has been reported and is increasing in some regions; C. tertium is resistant to penicillin, cephalosporins, and clindamycin - good anaerobic susceptibility testing matters (p.1242-1243).

management: Perform immediate, radical surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue, extending to amputation when required, as the single most life-saving intervention
Start high-dose intravenous antibiotics, combining a penicillin with clindamycin for its antitoxin, protein-synthesis-inhibiting effect
Deliver aggressive fluid resuscitation and organ support in intensive care for the accompanying septic shock
Consider adjunctive hyperbaric oxygen therapy where available, without delaying surgery
Return for repeat surgical exploration and debridement, since the necrotic margin can advance rapidly despite antibiotics
In survivors of spontaneous C. septicum myonecrosis, investigate the gastrointestinal tract for occult malignancy such as colonic cancer
Coordinate surgery, intensive care and infectious diseases input, with attention to tetanus prophylaxis and wound care

cells.text: Resect to viable tissue; amputation if needed; re-explore
Clindamycin suppresses toxin; clindamycin alone inadequate
Close after 5 to 6 days when free of infection
